cards.title: Regulator warns home insurers to improve their claims handling processes
cards.claim: FSRA's first home insurance claims review of 20 insurers flagged slow settlement and urged insurers to keep improving claims handling because delays strain consumers financially.

stat.what: average time to settle an Ontario home claim across 20 insurers, about 97% of market

cards.relevance: Gives the Ontario supervisory benchmark and tone against which 30-day large-claim and 13-day small-claim medians can be read.
cards.limit: Secondary press report; period definition (2019 vs 2019-2022) varies by outlet and the FSRA primary page returned 403.

cards.title: FSRA calls for improvement of P&C claims handling after review
cards.claim: FSRA named five improvement areas: settlement-time variability, proof-of-loss use, adjuster oversight, denial tracking and customer communication, so timeliness is a supervised conduct theme, not just an efficiency goal.
cards.relevance: Shows regulator expectations cover adjuster oversight and communication, so any authority or fast-track change must keep those controls.
cards.limit: Press summary; no numeric timeline standard stated; does not cover Québec.

cards.title: AMF Sound Commercial Practices Guideline (insurers)
cards.claim: Search snippets indicate the AMF guideline has a claims examination and settlement section and expects delegation-of-authority rules, but page text was not retrievable.
cards.relevance: Primary Québec source needed for Team C; expectations on who may reject claims at each delegation level bear on authority design.
cards.limit: Page returned 403; content known only from search snippets and a law-firm summary, no verified number.

cards.title: J.D. Power 2024 US Property Claims Satisfaction Study (via Insurance-Canada.ca)
cards.claim: Homeowners claim cycle times lengthened, and digital reporters finished far faster than non-digital ones, with satisfaction falling sharply for claims that dragged past a month.

stat.value: 23.9 days overall; 34.2 catastrophe; about 15 digital vs 28 non-digital
stat.what: average days from claim report to finished repairs

cards.relevance: External property cycle-time benchmark and evidence that digital intake and process, not headcount alone, drive speed.
cards.limit: US data, report-to-repair measure, not Canadian water claims or closure date.

cards.title: J.D. Power 2025 US Auto Claims Satisfaction Study (via Claims Journal)
cards.claim: Auto repair cycle times fell year over year as claim volumes eased, while vehicles with more driver-assistance features took longer to repair.

stat.what: average repair cycle time for repairable vehicles

cards.relevance: Shows cycle time moves with claim volume and shop capacity, relevant to Team C's intake doubling.
cards.limit: US repair-shop cycle time, not insurer claim-close time; not Canadian.

cards.title: Adjuster Authority in Insurance Claims
cards.claim: Authority is tiered by role, with experienced adjusters settling roughly $20k-$50k and larger amounts escalating to supervisors or committees, which stalls payments when the adjuster cannot decide.

stat.what: typical settlement authority of experienced adjusters before escalation

cards.relevance: Illustrates how a threshold-based escalation like the $10k senior-review rule creates handoffs and queueing.
cards.limit: Policyholder-side law-firm blog; thresholds anecdotal and insurer-specific figures are confidential.

cards.title: California FAIR Plan claims: adjuster authority and payment approval (Insurance Journal)
cards.claim: Commentary attributes claim delays partly to authority concentrated high in the organization, slow manager responses to payment-authority requests and overburdened adjusters, and recommends clearer authority ladders.
cards.relevance: Directly challenges 'just hire adjusters' by naming authority bottlenecks and approval lag as cycle-time drag.
cards.limit: Opinion piece on one troubled insurer; no caseload or timing metrics given.

cards.title: Industry survey: claims department challenges and AI
cards.claim: Milliman, citing the Rising study, reports heavy caseloads and turnover, and that high-performing claims organizations use workflow automation and predictive analytics more than low performers.

stat.what: high vs low performing claims organizations using workflow automation; and about 10% of claims drive 90% of costs

cards.relevance: Supports triage and automation alongside staffing, and the 10%-of-claims concentration echoes the senior-review pattern.
cards.limit: Largely workers' compensation context; caseload figures (50-75 complex, 111 max) are not property benchmarks.

cards.title: Insurance claims transformation
cards.claim: Homeowners claims handled digitally, with online notice and photo-based assessment, reached payment faster than conventional claims, and automation frees adjusters for complex work.

stat.what: faster time to payment for digitally processed homeowners claims

cards.relevance: Quantifies the benefit of a digital fast-track for low-complexity claims, the main alternative to adding adjusters.
cards.limit: Pandemic-era US data; no industry straight-through share; consultancy framing.

cards.title: Claims 2030: Dream or reality? (McKinsey)
cards.claim: Search snippets say simple claims with predictable patterns can be fully straight-through processed while complex claims diverge, but the page fetch timed out.
cards.relevance: Conceptual authority for splitting simple from complex claims, as the $10k senior-review split does.
cards.limit: Fetch timed out; wording unverified beyond search snippet; no figures read.

cards.title: Scaling for crisis: how the insurance industry is reinventing catastrophe response
cards.claim: Crawford Canada describes a surge model of full-time core adjusters, a deployable cat roster and a contracted pool of retirees, with most 2024 cat claims handled remotely.
cards.relevance: Shows flexible surge capacity as an alternative to permanent hires for Team C's intake spike.
cards.limit: Vendor perspective from an independent adjusting firm selling surge capacity.

cards.title: Insurers bring cat claims in-house: how independent adjusters adapt
cards.claim: Major Canadian insurers are shifting more claims in-house for consistency and customer experience while still using independent adjusters for surges and specialized or rural claims.

stat.what: share of claims Travelers Canada handles in-house

cards.relevance: Describes the in-house versus independent adjuster mix Canadian peers use for peak load.
cards.limit: Qualitative trade reporting; no cycle-time or cost comparison.

cards.title: It's time to break down artificial barriers that impact claims response
cards.claim: IBC argues provincially fragmented adjuster licensing and temporary out-of-province permissions limit surge capacity as weather-related claims have nearly doubled over a decade.

stat.what: increase in weather-related claims, from about 694,000 (2004-2013) to over 1.3 million in the last 10 years

cards.relevance: Shows adjuster supply is constrained by structure, not only headcount, and that Québec staff cannot easily be backfilled from other provinces.
cards.limit: Industry lobby advocacy piece; catastrophe focus, not routine water claims.
